case_study_insert.main_stem: Cocoa Bloom Chocolate (CBC) is a public limited company in the confectionery sector, based near the Pacific coast and employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2005 by Elena Vasquez, it supplies premium chocolate bars to export distributors and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. CBC plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new tempering and moulding line, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. CBC faces rising quality complaints about inconsistent tempering and absenteeism has reached 7%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The moulding line produced 31,200 bars last quarter with a waste rate of 5.4%, up from 3.9% a year ago. Quality complaints rose from 26 to 41 per month. Average delivery lead time is 5.6 days. A survey of 750 consumers found that 61% would pay up to $0.60 more for single-origin cocoa bars, and 55% read sustainability labels. Skills records show 18 of 60 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the tempering machines; off-the-job courses at the coastal technical institute cost $1,250 per employee. HR is weighing internal promotion against external recruitment for two new tempering supervisor posts.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Cocoa Bloom Chocolate as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $11.80 to $12.65 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale cocoa bean prices have risen 14.3% year-on-year, food inflation is 5.9%, and consumer spending on premium chocolate grew 4.1%.

questions.question_text: CBC plans to fund part of its tempering-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CBC of using a share issue to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $700,000 share issue brings in permanent equity that never has to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, protecting cash flow while CBC carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a variable cost of $7.50 a unit. Unlike the $500,000 bank loan, dividends can be reduced or delayed if export demand weakens, so the new tempering line can absorb the 5.4% waste rate without the pressure of a fixed monthly repayment as the 3.75%-to-4.5% rate rise feeds through.

Point 2: Equity strengthens the balance sheet of this public limited company, leaving more headroom to borrow later and signalling confidence to export distributors and investors. Because CBC already has 60 staff and 18 of them still need tempering training, avoiding loan covenants gives management freedom to spend on quality improvement and on the $1,200,000 moulding project without a lender restricting how the capital is used. Retaining the $500,000 loan facility for working capital also gives flexibility the share issue alone cannot provide.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CBC and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CBC is launching a new single-origin cocoa range. Consider national television advertising, in-store demonstrations, or social media influencer marketing. Which should CBC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would reach millions of consumers quickly and could support the premium price for single-origin bars supplied to export distributors. However, airtime is very expensive for a company deploying $1,200,000 on a tempering line, and the 61% of 750 surveyed consumers who would pay $0.60 more are a specific segment that mass TV reaches only expensively and wastefully. TV also cannot explain sustainability labels in depth.

In-store demonstrations: Tastings in the retailers that stock CBC's bars let consumers experience the tempering quality directly and can convert the 55% who read sustainability labels at the point of sale. The limit is scale: demonstrations are labour-intensive for a 60-person workforce already short of trained tempering operators, and they cannot reach export distributors or consumers who shop elsewhere.

Social media influencer marketing: Food reviewers can show the tempering finish and single-origin story visually to a targeted audience, with measurable clicks and a lower cost than TV. Credibility must be managed and results build gradually, but the reach is national and the 61% premium segment can be addressed precisely.

Recommendation: CBC should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by a small number of in-store demonstrations. It targets the researched premium segment at a fraction of TV's cost and works for export-facing brand awareness. Television is rejected as costly and untargeted given the $500,000 loan commitment and 5.4% waste rate; demonstrations alone are rejected as too labour-intensive to scale with 18 staff still needing training.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CBC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CBC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and demonstrations are rejected.

questions.question_text: CBC's absenteeism has reached 7% and tempering quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for CBC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 employees a real voice in how the new tempering and moulding line is organised, which helps satisfy esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Operators who help set moulding routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking CBC's 7% absenteeism rate and making best use of the flat organisational structure rather than imposing solutions from above.

Point 2: Consulting the people who handle the tempering machines daily generates practical ideas that can reduce the 5.4% waste rate and the rise in quality complaints from 26 to 41 per month. Higher involvement builds commitment and can lower labour turnover, protecting the 31,200 bars packed last quarter and the $13.50 selling price while the $1,200,000 line beds in and the 18 untrained staff are brought up to standard.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CBC's absenteeism, waste and output.

questions.question_text: CBC needs two new tempering supervisors. Consider internal promotion or external recruitment. Which should CBC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal promotion: Promoting from the existing 60-strong workforce rewards loyal staff, needs no advertising or agency fees and shortens induction because the candidate already knows CBC's tempering standards. It also supports democratic leadership by showing a clear career path, which can help reduce 7% absenteeism. The drawback is that the pool is limited: 18 of 60 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the tempering machines, so an internal appointee may lack the formal skills to cut the 5.4% waste rate.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced tempering supervisors from outside brings proven expertise and a fresh approach to the 26-to-41 rise in quality complaints, and external candidates can be appointed specifically for the $1,200,000 moulding line. The costs are higher, induction takes longer, and an outsider may not fit CBC's flat, participative culture or understand its export-distributor requirements.

Decision: CBC should choose internal promotion for one post and external recruitment for the other. The internal appointment motivates staff and exploits existing knowledge of the line; the external hire supplies the specialist tempering skill that 18 untrained operators lack. Choosing only internal candidates is rejected because it would not close the skills gap behind the 5.4% waste rate, while choosing only outsiders is rejected because it would ignore staff development and worsen morale when absenteeism is already 7%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment methods with limited application to CBC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of CBC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both recruitment methods in the context of CBC with a well-justified decision covering skills, cost and morale.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CBC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($13.50 − $7.50) = $420,000 ÷ $6.00 = 70,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 70,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CBC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 70,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, to judge whether the $1,200,000 tempering line is justified.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets CBC test a retailer discount: a $0.60 concession would leave $5.40, so managers can see whether extra volume still covers fixed costs of $420,000.
3. The figures set the sales target needed to service interest on the $500,000 bank loan before further capital is committed.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $420,000 ÷ 120,000 + $7.50 = $11.00, and labour productivity as 120,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 2,000 units per worker, providing benchmarks to attack the 5.4% waste rate and the 14.3% cocoa-price rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 70,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 50,000 units vs 120,000 output; discount modelling against $420,000 fixed costs; loan servicing on the $500,000 bank loan; and unit cost of $11.00 with labour productivity of 2,000 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CBC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CBC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $540,000; 2025 current assets = $245,000 + $230,000 + $95,000 = $570,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $540,000 ÷ $360,000 = 1.50 and 2025 = $570,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.90. Excluding inventories gives 2024 = ($540,000 − $210,000) ÷ $360,000 = $330,000 ÷ $360,000 = 0.92 and 2025 = ($570,000 − $245,000) ÷ $300,000 = $325,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened sharply. The 2024 figure of 1.50 rose to 1.90 because current liabilities fell from $360,000 to $300,000 while current assets rose to $570,000, helped by cash increasing from $70,000 to $95,000. The inventory-excluding measure improved from 0.92 to 1.08, so CBC is less dependent on selling chocolate stock to meet short-term debts while it services a $500,000 bank loan and a $1,200,000 expansion. There are caveats: inventories rose from $210,000 to $245,000, which may reflect slow-moving stock given the 5.4% waste rate, and receivables, although lower at $230,000, still tie up cash that could fund the 18 staff still needing training.

Conclusion: CBC's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency and the improvement does not rest on inventory alone. The remaining risk is higher stock, so waste control should be tightened as the new tempering line starts up.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CBC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CBC of introducing single-origin cocoa sourcing for its premium bars.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Single-origin sourcing supports the premium positioning that 61% of 750 surveyed consumers are willing to pay $0.60 more for, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit even while cocoa bean prices rise 14.3%. It also gives CBC a clearer sustainability story for the 55% who read labels, strengthening its appeal to export distributors and the $1,200,000 tempering investment.

Disadvantage: Single-origin beans are usually scarcer and more expensive than blended beans, which would push up the $7.50 variable cost per unit unless the $0.60 premium is fully accepted by consumers and retailers. Supply is also less reliable: a poor harvest in one origin could interrupt the 31,200-bar quarterly run rate and worsen the 5.4% waste rate, while fixed costs of $420,000 remain regardless of throughput.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CBC's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 14.3% rise in cocoa bean prices will affect CBC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): The base rate increases by 0.75 percentage points. If the $500,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year, which is small next to fixed costs of $420,000 a year; if the loan is fixed-rate it is zero. Higher rates might dampen consumer spending on premium chocolate, but CBC can largely remove the direct risk by fixing the loan rate, and the $700,000 share issue reduces reliance on debt.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $11.80 to $12.65 per hour): This raises CBC's wage bill for a workforce of 60 and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The honest comparison uses productivity derived from the insert: 120,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 2,000 units per worker. If that productivity is maintained the rise is absorbable; if output falls because 18 staff remain untrained, unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution per unit narrows.

Cocoa bean price rise (14.3%): The insert does not decompose the $7.50 variable cost, so only a labelled bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 14.3%, the increase is 0.143 × $7.50 = $1.07 per unit, and at 120,000 units a year that is about $128,700. That is an upper bound rather than a forecast; the real figure depends on how much of the $7.50 is cocoa, which is not given. CBC can pass part on through the $0.60 premium that 61% of surveyed consumers accept.

Conclusion: The 14.3% cocoa price rise will have the greatest impact. It applies to every bar and threatens the $6.00 contribution underlying the $1,200,000 expansion, whereas the interest cost of $3,750 is small and fixable and the wage rise can be offset if 2,000-units-per-worker productivity holds. Input-cost inflation therefore demands the strongest response.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CBC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CBC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CBC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
